issues.legal_issue: A requirement to obtain court permission for the sale of a minor’s share does not make the entire sale agreement contingent when the agreement does not provide that denial of permission terminates it and the other vendors can convey their distinct shares.
material_facts: The agreement required the sellers to obtain permission to sell a minor’s share but did not state that the agreement would become invalid if permission were refused.
The permission application was refused during the suit.
The other sellers held distinct shares that they could transfer.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was not a contingent contract that failed in its entirety; the sellers’ transferable shares remained capable of being conveyed.
issues.legal_principle: The agreement must be read according to its terms; a permission requirement does not itself make the whole agreement contingent where there is no term providing for termination on refusal and some vendors can convey their own interests. The Court distinguished Dalsukh M. Pancholi v. The Guarantee Life and Employment Insurance Co. Ltd. and Others, where court approval was an essential condition and the vendor could not convey his own interest without it, and HPA International v. Bhagwandas Fatehchand Daswani, where the agreement expressly provided for cancellation if sanction was not obtained.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A purchaser brought a suit seeking performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.permission_requirement_lacks_termination: The agreement required permission for a part of the sale but did not state that refusal would terminate the agreement.
predicates.vendors_hold_transferable_distinct_share: Some vendors held distinct interests that they could transfer without the required permission.

issues.definition: When a purchaser seeks performance and the agreement contains no termination term for refused permission while some vendors can transfer distinct shares, the remaining contract is not contingent.

issues.legal_issue: Specific performance may be granted for the performable part of a contract when the seller cannot perform the whole, the purchaser accepts exclusion of the unperformable part, and the purchaser satisfies the applicable consideration and relinquishment requirements.
material_facts: A minor held a share in the property, and the court refused permission to sell that share during the suit.
The other sellers could convey their own shares.
The purchaser sought a sale of the other sellers’ shares, relinquished any claim to the minor’s share, and sought to pay the consideration reduced by the proportionate value of that share.
The purchaser was found to have been ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was entitled to specific performance of the part of the agreement that the sellers could perform, excluding the minor’s share and adjusting the consideration accordingly.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12(3) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits specific performance of the part a defaulting party can perform when the other party meets the applicable payment requirement and relinquishes claims to performance and compensation for the unperformed part. The Court relied on Sardar Singh v. Krishna Devi (Smt.) and Another and Rachakonda Narayana v. Ponthala Parvathamma and Another; Rachakonda states that specific performance is ordinarily granted when the statutory requirements are met, unless delay, laches, or another disability exists. The Court also considered Surinder Singh v. Kapoor Singh (Dead) through LRs. and Others.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and seller_cannot_perform_entire_contract and seller_can_transfer_performable_part and buyer_relinquishes_unperformable_part and buyer_pays_adjusted_consideration and buyer_ready_and_willing

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A purchaser brought a suit seeking specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.seller_cannot_perform_entire_contract: A seller was unable to convey the whole property covered by the agreement.
predicates.seller_can_transfer_performable_part: The seller could convey a distinct part of the agreed property.
predicates.buyer_relinquishes_unperformable_part: The purchaser gave up claims to performance and compensation concerning the part that could not be conveyed.
predicates.buyer_pays_adjusted_consideration: The purchaser offered to pay the agreed consideration adjusted as required for the part to be conveyed.
predicates.buyer_ready_and_willing: The purchaser remained ready and willing to perform the purchaser’s obligations.

issues.definition: If a purchaser seeking specific performance meets the stated conditions for the part the seller can convey, specific performance is granted for that part.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser seeking specific performance may also obtain partition and separate possession of the share to be conveyed, and partition relief is ordinarily ancillary to the specific-performance decree.
material_facts: The purchaser amended the claim to seek partition of the property, excluding the minor’s share, as well as conveyance and possession of the other sellers’ shares.
The trial court granted a preliminary decree for partition along with relief concerning specific performance.
The decree concerning the minor’s share had not been appealed by the minor and had attained finality.
issues.conclusion: The partition relief could be granted in addition to specific performance; ordinarily, final partition proceedings should follow execution and registration of the sale deed rather than precede it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 22(1)(a) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 allows a plaintiff to claim partition and separate possession in a suit for specific performance, thereby avoiding multiplicity of proceedings. The Court relied on Babu Lal v. M/s. Hazari Lal Kishori Lal and Others. It observed that partition relief is incidental or ancillary to the main relief and that final partition proceedings should ordinarily begin after the sale deed under the specific-performance decree is executed and registered.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A purchaser brought a suit seeking specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.purchaser_claims_partition_and_separate_: The purchaser requested partition and separate possession in the suit.
predicates.purchaser_limits_claim_to_conveyable_sha: The purchaser limited the requested partition and possession to the share that could be conveyed, excluding the unavailable share.

issues.definition: When a purchaser seeking specific performance also requests partition and separate possession limited to the conveyable share, partition relief may accompany specific performance.

issues.legal_issue: An alternative claim for refund of an advance and damages does not by itself bar a decree for specific performance, and discretionary relief need not be refused without a demonstrated reason to deny it.
material_facts: The purchaser sought specific performance and also pleaded an alternative claim for refund and damages.
The opposing parties had not raised the discretionary-relief objection before the High Court.
The Court found no reason shown, having regard to the parties’ conduct, for refusing discretionary relief.
issues.conclusion: The alternative claim for refund and damages did not bar specific performance, and no demonstrated basis justified refusing the discretionary relief.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 concerns the court’s discretion to grant specific performance. The Court rejected the objection because it had not been raised before the High Court and no basis for refusing relief had been shown; an alternative prayer for refund and damages is not itself a bar to specific performance.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A purchaser brought a suit seeking specific performance of a sale agreement.
predicates.alternative_refund_or_damages_claimed: The purchaser also sought refund or damages as an alternative remedy.
predicates.no_case_specific_equitable_bar_shown: The opposing party did not establish a case-specific reason to refuse discretionary relief.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, an alternative claim for refund or damages does not bar specific performance when no case-specific equitable bar is shown.

issues.legal_issue: A person bound by a decree concerning that person’s interests may be a proper party to an appeal even if no specific-performance decree was made against that person, without being a necessary party.
material_facts: Two persons added to the appeal were bound by the trial court’s decree.
No specific-performance decree had been made against those added persons.
The decree concerning one added person’s share had attained finality because that person had not appealed.
issues.conclusion: The added persons were proper parties to the appeal, though they were not necessary parties.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished between necessary and proper parties in light of the effect of the decree on the added persons. Their being bound by the trial court’s decree made them proper parties even though no specific-performance decree had been passed against them.

predicates.appeal_concerns_decree_affecting_persons: An appeal concerns a decree that affects the interests of persons who were not appellants in the lower-court appeal.
predicates.persons_are_bound_by_trial_decree: Those persons are bound by the trial court’s decree.
predicates.no_specific_performance_decree_against_p: The trial court did not make a specific-performance decree against those persons.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a decree affecting persons who are bound by it but against whom specific performance was not ordered, those persons are proper but not necessary parties.
